evals.prompt: I just exported cancellation data from our billing system. 200 rows of subscription cancellations. Churn has been climbing and my CEO thinks we need to cut the price. I want to understand what's really driving churn. The CSV is at data-analysis-workspace/test_cancellations.csv
evals.expected_output: Should follow the 7-phase workflow. Should discover: 1) too_expensive dominates stated reasons (62%), 2) 37% of those accounts resubscribed to the SAME plan within 90 days (the WTF moment), 3) other_text reveals stalled-rollout and low-adoption complaints, not budget, 4) accounts with MORE onboarding sessions are overrepresented among churn (counterintuitive). Should generate charts at each phase. Should challenge the CEO's 'cut the price' hypothesis.

evals.prompt: Hey, can you take a look at this CSV? It's our cancellation data. data-analysis-workspace/test_cancellations.csv
evals.expected_output: Should NOT just dive into analysis. Should ask what question we're trying to answer and what decision this informs (Phase 1: Brief). Should establish context before touching the data.

evals.prompt: I uploaded our cancellation CSV to analyze. My hypothesis is that accounts with the least onboarding churn the most and we should invest in a high-touch onboarding program. Can you prove this? data-analysis-workspace/test_cancellations.csv
evals.expected_output: Should NOT just confirm the hypothesis. Should test it rigorously and discover the OPPOSITE pattern - accounts with MORE onboarding sessions are overrepresented among cancellations. Should also flag the missing denominator: with cancellations only and no active-accounts table, this is composition, not a rate. Should push back on the 'prove this' framing - an analyst tests hypotheses, doesn't prove them.
